definition: ADS-B sent on 1090 MHz by a Mode S transponder; required in US Class A airspace and the standard outside the US.
A carrier switching off its 3G network; AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon did so between February 2022 and January 2023.
Text messaging between aircraft and airlines, created by ARINC in 1978, carried on VHF, HF and satellite links.
A system in which aircraft broadcast their own position; a common thing to receive with an RTL-SDR.
Cockpit equipment that receives ADS-B and related traffic (TIS-B) and weather (FIS-B) services; not required in the US.
A database service that tells a higher-power 6 GHz Wi-Fi access point which channels it can use without harming licensed microwave links.
The VHF band, roughly 118-137 MHz, where US air traffic control and related services use 25 kHz channels; 121.5 MHz is for emergencies.
Ships broadcast identity, position and course on dedicated marine VHF channels so others can see them.
A decision about which kind of radio service may use a band; assignments must follow the allocation table.
Radio that carries sound by varying the strength of a carrier; US stations are assigned 540-1600 kHz in 10 kHz steps.
A licensed, non-commercial radio service; US licenses are Technician, General and Amateur Extra, each by written exam.
Utility meters that report usage over a two-way network, often a radio mesh.
A place where many transmitting or receiving towers, antennas or dishes are clustered, usually on high ground, to share land, costs and backup.
The analog 137 MHz weather image signal from NOAA's legacy polar satellites, shut down in 2025.

aka: Amateur Radio on the International Space Station
definition: The program running the ISS ham radio station, used for school contacts and SSTV events.
The FCC's public registry of structures over 200 ft or near airports, searchable by coordinates and radius.
The number the FCC assigns to a registered structure; Media Bureau tools link stations to ASRNs within 0.5 km.
Permission for a specific station or licensee to use a specific frequency within an allocation.
An internet-protocol-based US TV broadcast standard that stations adopt voluntarily while keeping an ATSC 1.0 simulcast.
A database system that tells standard-power 6 GHz Wi-Fi access points which channels they can use without interfering with incumbent users.
FirstNet's 20 MHz of 700 MHz spectrum: 758-768 MHz downlink and 788-798 MHz uplink.

aka: Boston Area Police Emergency Radio Network
definition: Greater Boston's police mutual aid radio network, run by the Greater Boston Police Council since the early 1970s.
A small BLE transmitter that repeatedly broadcasts an ID so nearby phones can estimate how close they are.
A low-power form of Bluetooth introduced with version 4.0 in 2009, using 40 channels; used by wearables, trackers and beacons.
A device that connects a Thread mesh to a home Wi-Fi or Ethernet network.
The signal lost between the outside of a building and a point inside it; it rises with frequency and depends heavily on construction.
US mid-band 5G spectrum sold in Auction 107, which grossed $80.9 billion in 2021.
A unique station identifier such as W1MX; new UK Foundation call signs start M7 and Intermediate M8 or M9.
A tower with a wide top frame holding several stations' antennas side by side, like the Cabot Street tower in Needham.
A heart-shaped coverage pattern; WBZ's two Hull towers use one to cut signal over the Atlantic.
US mid-band spectrum at 3.5 GHz; the FCC auctioned 70 MHz of licensed CBRS spectrum in August 2020.
The antennas, radios and backhaul serving one coverage area; CTIA counted 418,887 US sites at end of 2021.
156.650 MHz, intership navigation safety; ships over 20 m keep a listening watch on it in US waters.
156.800 MHz, the international marine distress, safety and calling channel.
The MBTA's contactless fare card, introduced in 2006 and based on NXP MIFARE Classic.
The full AIS class required in the US on commercial vessels of 65 ft or more, larger towing vessels and others under 33 CFR 164.46.
A lighter AIS class that US rules allow on some fishing and smaller vessels.
An AM frequency where one high-power station is protected from interference over a wide area, day and night. WBZ 1030 is one.
Under Colorado law (C.R.S. 24-6-502), the policy a fully encrypted agency must adopt to give media access to primary dispatch channels.
A legal rule that certain vessels must use a state- or federally licensed local pilot, depending on type, size, flag and waters.
A radio system in which each group of users has its own dedicated frequency or channel.
Text messaging between controllers and pilots; required on new aircraft in Europe from 2014 under the Single European Sky rule.
The digital radio system used in the UK and much of Europe, where many stations share one transmitted multiplex.
A network of small antennas fed from a central head end, used in tunnels and large venues; the MBTA's dates from 2005.
Satellites that talk directly to ordinary mobile phones using mobile-network spectrum, such as Starlink's service for T-Mobile.
Two or more AM towers fed together so the signal is stronger in some directions and weaker in others, as at WBZ's Hull site.
A network of small antennas fed over fiber from a central point, used to carry cell signals into tunnels and buildings.
The apparent change in a satellite's frequency as it approaches and recedes; ISS SSTV listeners allow plus or minus 3 kHz.
Digital marine calling on channel 70 (156.525 MHz), with no voice.
The unpaired slice between mobile uplink and downlink in the US 600 MHz band; 653-657 MHz is licensed and 657-663 MHz unlicensed for mics.
The fraction of time a transmitter is actually sending; about 0.21% for the BC Hydro smart meters studied.
The legacy trunked radio system the MBTA is replacing with P25.
ITU band 11, 30-300 GHz, also called millimetric waves.
Transmitter power including antenna gain, counted as if radiated equally in all directions; US mic limits are stated in EIRP.
The US system that interrupts radio and TV with alerts; it replaced the Emergency Broadcast System between 1994 and 1997.
Ways of sharing spectrum: separate frequencies for each user (FDMA, P25 Phase 1) or separate time slots on one frequency (TDMA, P25 Phase 2).
The US agency created by the Communications Act of 1934 that administers the non-Federal Table of Frequency Allocations.
The five-member commission created by the Radio Act of 1927; replaced by the FCC in 1934.
The US nationwide broadband network for first responders, created by Congress in 2012 and built by AT&T under a 25-year contract.
Radio that carries sound by varying the carrier's frequency; the US band is 88-108 MHz with 200 kHz channels starting at 88.1 MHz.
A 38 kHz signal inside an FM channel carrying left-minus-right audio, while the main carrier carries left-plus-right for mono radios.
A range of frequencies with a lower and upper edge, such as 3.7-3.98 GHz; its width is its bandwidth.
The person who assigns a non-conflicting frequency to every wireless device at an event; the NFL uses SBE volunteer coordinators.
Ground stations at an airport that refine GPS for landing approaches; one at Newark was disrupted by a jammer in 2012.
The general term for satellite navigation systems such as GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou.
NOAA's geostationary weather satellites; GOES-19 became GOES East on April 7, 2025.
The US satellite navigation system, developed, maintained and operated by the US Space Force.
A buffer slice of spectrum between services; part of the US 600 MHz guard band (614-616 MHz) is open to unlicensed mics.
A slender tower held upright by steel guy cables anchored around it. WBZ-TV's Cedar Street tower in Needham is guyed.
A measure of a broadcast antenna's height relative to the average ground around it; WGBH-TV's is 362.7 m (1,190 ft).
Passing a phone's connection from one cell to the next as it moves; the 1983 Chicago system used computers to do this.
The US digital radio system, approved by the FCC in 2002, which adds digital sidebands next to an existing AM or FM signal.
One cycle per second; the unit of frequency. Radio frequencies are given in kilohertz, megahertz and gigahertz.
The IARC category RF fields were placed in in 2011, based on limited evidence; IARC says the label has no quantitative significance.
The unique aircraft address broadcast by a transponder; for US aircraft the FAA ties it to the tail number.

aka: International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection
definition: The body that publishes international RF exposure guidelines; its 2020 guidelines cover 100 kHz to 300 GHz, including 5G.
A wireless earpiece system that sends a performer their own mix; it shares the wireless mic bands and rules.
The 2016-2017 FCC auction in which TV stations sold spectrum and wireless carriers bought it; gross proceeds were $19.8 billion.
The UN agency, with 194 member governments, that maintains the Radio Regulations treaty.
Frequencies set aside for machines such as microwave ovens that use radio energy for non-communication purposes; unlicensed radios share them and must tolerate the noise.
The contactless card standard for tap cards, with a range up to about 10 cm.
The ITU allocation region that includes the 50 US states; the US Table of Frequency Allocations is based on it.
Drowning out a radio signal with noise so it cannot be received; GPS jammers have no lawful use in the US, per the FCC.
The three GPS carrier frequencies: 1575.42 MHz, 1227.6 MHz and 1176.45 MHz.
FAA program that makes FAA-fed flight-tracking vendors hide a registration from public display; it does not affect the ADS-B broadcast.
Push-to-talk two-way radio used by police, fire, EMS, utilities, transit and railroads, built from handhelds, vehicle radios, base stations and repeaters.
A long-range, slow, low-power chirp spread spectrum radio (LoRa) and the network protocol on top of it (LoRaWAN).
Energy-saving window glass with a thin metallic coating that reflects radio signals, causing far more loss than ordinary glass.
The FCC licensed category (Part 74 Subpart H) for wireless mics and related devices, which has secondary status and must protect TV broadcasters.
A hardware ID broadcast by a radio such as Bluetooth, which roadside readers can log to measure travel times.
One broadcast antenna shared by several stations, such as the six-bay panel antenna on the Prudential mast.
A common smart-home application standard, launched in 2022, that runs over Wi-Fi, Thread or Ethernet and uses BLE for setup.
Devices that relay each other's messages so data can hop around obstacles to reach a hub.
Locating an aircraft by comparing when its signal reaches four or more receivers (time difference of arrival); works only from roughly 3,000-10,000 ft and above.
Very high 5G frequencies (24, 28, 37, 39 and 47 GHz in the US) with large capacity and short range.
A transponder mode that gives each aircraft a unique address; aircraft with only Mode S are located by trackers using multilateration.
A Wi-Fi 7 feature that lets a device use more than one band at the same time.
Satellite signals reflected off buildings or walls before reaching a receiver, a cause of position errors.
One transmitted signal that bundles several radio or TV services; the UK had 75 small-scale DAB multiplexes by September 2025.
The Commerce Department agency that administers the Federal Table of Frequency Allocations for federal government users.
A 12-bit code on each conventional P25 packet that replaces the analog CTCSS and DCS tones of older radios.
A company that owns a tunnel or in-building network and lets several carriers share it.
A 13.56 MHz tap-range link used by phones, bank cards and transit cards; the card is powered by the reader.
The National Weather Service's 24-hour broadcast network on seven VHF channels from 162.400 to 162.550 MHz.
A shortwave station broadcasting coded numbers or tones of unconfirmed purpose; UVB-76 on 4625 kHz is the best known.
The FCC guide to evaluating compliance with its RF exposure limits.
The North American digital public safety radio standard, established in 1989 so radios from different makers can interoperate.
The version of P25 that splits one 12.5 kHz channel into two time slots, doubling voice capacity; approved in November 2010.
The FCC rules that let people use low-power radios without a license, provided they cause no harmful interference and accept any they receive.
A measure of transmitter output used in UK amateur power limits: 25 W Foundation, 100 W Intermediate, 1000 W Full.
A power-grid sensor that timestamps voltage and current readings with GPS-derived time.
A temporary ICAO address not linked to the owner in the US Civil Aircraft Registry, valid in US-managed airspace.
The UK and European term for wireless mics, IEMs and production radio, licensed in the UK by Ofcom.
NOAA's legacy polar-orbiting weather satellites (NOAA-15, -18, -19), decommissioned in 2025.
A service printed in capital letters in the US allocation table; it is protected from interference by secondary services.
Coaxial cable with slots that let radio signal leak out along its length, used in tunnels like the MBTA's.
An aircraft instrument that measures height above the ground by radio; the FAA found in 2021 that C-band 5G could interfere with some.
Scrambling digital voice so only radios holding the key can hear it; an optional feature of P25.
A clock that sets itself from a radio time signal such as WWVB; NIST prefers this name to 'atomic clock'.

term: readily accessible to the general public
definition: The Wiretap Act test for radio that may lawfully be intercepted; encrypted traffic does not meet it.
The move of US TV stations to new channels after the incentive auction, over 39 months in ten phases, finished in 2020.
A radio at a high site that receives a transmission and rebroadcasts it to extend range.
Tags read by radio, either passive (powered by the reader) or active (with a battery, like a toll tag).
Satellite-guided flight procedures that let planes fly precise, repeatable paths; at Logan they concentrated flight tracks.
A precise satellite-guided procedure that can include curved segments, used on Logan's Runway 33L approach since 2021.
A USB TV-tuner dongle built on the Realtek RTL2832U chip, used as a cheap wideband receiver (about 24-1766 MHz with common tuners).
An FAA advisory to airlines and pilots; SAFO 24002 (2024) covers GPS/GNSS disruptions.
Digital codes on NOAA Weather Radio that activate only receivers set for a given county or marine area.
How much RF energy body tissue absorbs, in W/kg; the US phone limit is 1.6 W/kg over 1 g of tissue.
US broadcast engineering society whose volunteer coordinators run game-day frequency coordination with the NFL.
A receiver that steps through many frequencies to find active transmissions; in the US it may not be able to receive cellular frequencies.
A service printed in normal type in the US table; it must not interfere with primary services and cannot claim protection from them.
The Communications Act provision that generally allows listening to radio but restricts divulging or profiting from what is heard.
ITU band 10, 3-30 GHz, also called centimetric waves.
An EASA safety advisory; SIB 2022-02 covers GNSS outages and alterations.
Several transmitter sites sending the same signal at once to cover a wide area, as BAPERN does.
AM signal that bounces off the upper atmosphere at night and comes down hundreds of miles away.
A low-power cell site on a pole or building that adds capacity in a small area; Crown Castle had more than 115,000 in 2022.

aka: International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea
definition: The international convention whose Chapter V Regulation 19 requires AIS on ships of 300 GT and up on international voyages and on all passenger ships.
Sale of spectrum licenses to the highest bidder; the FCC has held them since Congress authorized them in 1993.
Broadcasting fake satellite signals so a receiver computes a false position or time.
The four-digit transponder code assigned by air traffic control, also carried in ADS-B.
Still pictures sent as audio tones over a voice radio channel; the ISS sends them on 145.800 MHz FM during events.
SpaceX's second-generation Starlink satellites; the FCC has authorized 15,000 of them as of January 2026.
A study that gathers and grades all relevant research on a question by a preset method, like the 2024 WHO-commissioned Karipidis review.
The 470-512 MHz band used for public safety radio in some large US metro areas, including Greater Boston.
A virtual channel on a trunked system that a group of users joins; a control channel assigns it a real frequency for each conversation.
A low-power IPv6 mesh radio for smart-home devices, using the same 802.15.4 radio as Zigbee.
A battery-powered sensor in each wheel that radios tire pressure to the car, required on new US vehicles from the 2008 model year.
Finding a position from measured distances to several known points; a GPS receiver uses distances to satellites.
A computer-controlled radio system that assigns each conversation a free channel from a shared pool.
US-only ADS-B on 978 MHz, accepted below 18,000 ft and the only link carrying free FIS-B weather.
ITU band 9, 300-3,000 MHz, also called decimetric waves.
The FCC's public database of wireless licenses, searchable by call sign, name, location, ASR number or frequency.
Radio use allowed without an individual license, but with no protection from interference.
A street lined with tall buildings that block and reflect satellite signals.
How far off a satellite's own distance information is before a receiver adds its own errors; the US commits to 2.0 m or less, 95% of the time.
A digital VHF datalink at 31.5 kbit/s on twelve channels from 136.700 to 136.975 MHz, carrying ACARS and CPDLC.
ITU band 8, 30-300 MHz, also called metric waves.
The channel number a TV displays, which can differ from the RF channel the signal uses. WBZ-TV is virtual 4 on RF 20.
The Wi-Fi generation certified from January 2024, adding 320 MHz channels in 6 GHz, Multi-Link Operation and 4K QAM.
US alerts pushed to phones in a targeted area, launched in April 2012.
The UK offence of using a receiver with intent to learn the contents of a message you are not an intended recipient of, or disclosing it.
An ITU conference held every three to four years to revise the Radio Regulations; WRC-27 meets in Shanghai in 2027.
NIST shortwave time stations in Colorado and Hawaii that broadcast ticks and spoken time.
NIST's 60 kHz time-code station near Fort Collins, Colorado, which sets radio-controlled clocks.
A sub-GHz smart-home mesh radio at 908.42 MHz in the US and 868.42 MHz in Europe.
A low-power mesh smart-home radio built on IEEE 802.15.4, mainly at 2.4 GHz.
